newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada grain elevator turn ratios too low-Pioneer.
newsitem.headline: Canada grain elevator turn ratios too low-Pioneer.

text.p: Canada's grain storage space needs to be trimmed if grain handling firms are to recoup their capital costs on new elevators by turning inventory over more frequently, Pioneer Grain Co's president said.
"In my judgment, a reasonable return on investment is an eight- to 10-times turn ratio a year," Pioneer president Curt Vossen told Reuters in an interview.
There were 1,199 primary elevators on Canada's Prairies at the end of 1996/97 (Aug/July) down 10 percent from 1,333 elevators on Aug 1, 1995, Canadian Wheat Board figures show.

That date marked the end of Canada's 98-year-old rail grain freight rate subsidy, and that led to elevator and secondary rail line abandonment in favor of concrete high volume elevators along primary rail lines.
"A year ago in western Canada you had turn ratios of five to six times a year but for these new facilities to pay for themselves you've got to do it more often," he said.

Grainhandler Pioneer posted sales of C$1.3 billion in fiscal 1996 (Jan/Dec) compared to C$1 billion in 1995. It operated 125 elevators compared to 175 two years ago, down 28.5 percent. Pioneer opened two multi-million dollar high volume elevators in 1997.
Five more so-called high-through-put elevators were being built at costs of C$7 to C$10 million each with more projects to be announced, Vossen said.
Rivals Saskatchewan Wheat Pool, United Grain Growers Ltd, Alberta Wheat Pool and Manitoba Pool Elevators are all involved in multi-million dollar elevator projects.
